title: What happens at your first pelvic health physiotherapy appointment?
seoTitle: What happens at a first pelvic physio visit
description: A first pelvic-health physio visit starts with history and goals. Learn consent for optional exams, chaperones, and online versus in-person limits.
primaryQuestion: What happens at a pelvic health physiotherapy session?
directAnswer: A first visit centres on your story: when symptoms began, what aggravates or eases them, pregnancies or surgeries, bladder and bowel habits, and what you want to do again. The physiotherapist explains assessment options. An internal vaginal or rectal examination is offered only with clear consent and can be declined; a chaperone can be requested. You should leave with an initial plan, home strategies that match findings, and clarity on follow-up or medical referral. A first visit should not include a surprise procedure.

sections.heading: What to prepare before you arrive
paragraphs: POGP suggests arriving ready to describe when trouble began, what flares or settles it, earlier investigations, wider health, and how your job or hobbies load the pelvis. A short bladder diary over about three days (drinks, toilet visits, volumes if measured, urgency and leaks) helps if continence is the issue. Loose, comfortable clothes make movement screening easier.

Write questions in advance: Do I need an internal exam today? What can I do this week? When should I see a doctor instead? Bring a list of medicines and prior reports if you have them. You do not need perfect paperwork to be taken seriously.

sections.heading: How the conversation usually starts
paragraphs: UH Sussex describes a first pelvic-health appointment that gathers detail on urinary, gynaecological, bowel and obstetric history as relevant. NHS GGC notes that a specialist physiotherapist takes a detailed history, discusses concerns, and carries out an examination if appropriate, explaining steps so you can ask questions at any time.

Expect privacy and confidentiality. Say if topics feel difficult. Dr. Zalak Shah (PT) uses this history to decide whether physiotherapy is the right lane or whether medical review should come first for infection signs, unexplained bleeding or neurological red flags.

sections.heading: Examination choices, consent and chaperones
paragraphs: For bladder, bowel or pelvic-pain problems, an internal examination may be offered to assess pelvic-floor strength, coordination and tenderness. UH Sussex states the process is explained first, consent is required, you may refuse and still receive treatment, and a chaperone can be provided. POGP adds that you may take time to decide or bring a friend or family member.

Nothing should proceed because you feel awkward saying no. You can pause or stop during an examination. Coaching that stays outside the vagina, such as breathing drills, posture cues and practice clearing a cough, can still start when internal assessment is declined.

sections.heading: Online visits versus in-person care
paragraphs: Video appointments can cover history, education, bladder and bowel advice, and external movement coaching. They cannot include a hands-on internal pelvic-floor examination. If your goals depend on confirming contraction quality, tenderness mapping or prolapse findings, an in-person slot is the clearer route.
Hybrid care is common: education online, examination in clinic later. Ask which parts of your plan truly need travel and which can be reviewed remotely after the first assessment.

sections.heading: Goals, follow-up and referrals
paragraphs: Agree what success looks like in your own words: fewer leaks, less heaviness after standing, comfortable intimacy steps, or return to a chosen activity. NICE NG210 expects a management plan to be discussed and agreed, and supervised training programmes to include progress review during and at the end of the programme when that pathway is used.

POGP notes that if the problem seems outside physiotherapy scope, you may be directed to another professional such as your GP. Hand-off to a gynaecologist such as Dr. Charmi Shah fits when medical differentials dominate. Seek urgent medical care for retention with pain, fever with severe pelvic pain, or sudden continence change plus genital numbness or weak legs rather than waiting for the next therapy visit.

faqs.question: Will I have an internal examination on the first visit?
faqs.answer: Only if it is appropriate and you consent after an explanation. Many services offer it at a first or later visit. You can decline, postpone, or request a chaperone without losing access to other advice.

faqs.question: Can a family member interpret for me?
faqs.answer: UH Sussex strongly advises against using a family member or friend as interpreter and asks you to request a professional interpreter when needed. Ask the clinic how language support is arranged before the day.
